newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leoneans flee capital after fighting.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leoneans flee capital after fighting.

text.p: France evacuated more foreigners from Freetown on Wednesday and Sierra Leoneans streamed out to the provinces as Ghana tried to avert a showdown pitting Nigeria against coup leaders and their rebel allies.
Residents have virtually abandoned the seafront Aberdeen district, which was hit by shells on Monday, fleeing either into the city centre or to the interior.
Liberian refugees fled the Jui camp, which lies between the Nigerian base and positions of Sierra Leonean troops and rebels of the Revolutionary United Front.

Refugee spokesman Mac Varney Rogers said the camp's 5,000 population had moved to a disused airfield nearby where they were no longer in the line of fire but were sleeping in the open air. "When it rains, we get soaked," he said.

Ghana sent a team to try to negotiate a peaceful end to the showdown, which began with a coup on May 25 and turned bloody on Monday after Nigerian gunboats shelled the city and dissident soldiers and rebel allies turned on Nigerian soldiers there.

Ghana's deputy foreign minister, Victor Gbeho, and Brigadier Seth Obeng, chief of staff army headquarters, went to the Monrovia headquarters of the Nigerian-led ECOMOG West African force on Tuesday and were due in Freetown on Wednesday.

"If use of force becomes a last resort and is inevitable, it may have to come to that," U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters during a stopover in London, adding that the coup leaders lacked support at home and abroad.
"How they expect to survive I do not know. I wish they would be sensible and cut their losses and walk away," he said.

In a possible sign of hope, a spokesman for the coup leaders said they had freed some 300 Nigerian soldiers, whom they captured on Monday, to hold as human shields against air raids. They returned the Nigerians to their Freetown base.
"Both the military and the negotiated peaceful options are not mutually exclusive," Ghana's acting communications minister, Kofi Totobi-Quakyi, told state media in Accra.

All over town, families stood with bundles of belongings waiting for communal taxis to take them to truck parks on the edge of Freetown where they hoped to find a ride to the interior. Rebels roved around the city in looted vehicles.
Sierra Leone, a former British colony racked by civil war since 1991, has suffered three coups in five years. It is one of the world's poorest countries despite a wealth of minerals.
The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit called for the restoration of ousted civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe, the new OAU chairman, told the closing session of the summit in his capital Harare that Africa would not tolerate military takeovers in future.
"We unanimously and unreservedly condemned the coup d'etat in Sierra Leone as an enormous setback for democracy in Africa," he said.
Coup leaders put the death toll in the bombardment and fighting at 80. Other sources accused the military of exaggerating and said it was no more than 50.
The United States carried out its largest single-day non-combatant evacuation from the city on Tuesday, bringing out 1,261 civilians by helicopter to neighbouring Guinea.
The French navy brought out 261 foreign nationals on Wednesday in its second such operation since the coup.

Britain chartered a Boeing 747 to bring evacuees from the Guinea to London on Thursday. The Foreign Office said it would fly out about 200 British people, their dependants, 75 U.S. nationals and 80 others, mostly from European Union countries.
Kabbah, who won 1996 multi-party elections which ended four years of military rule, is in Guinea.
The coup leaders accused him of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, and of encouraging ethnic conflict.
Sankoh, named vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, is being held in Nigeria. He has told his men to back the coup.
